data.hypothesis: The catalog has three distinct valid programs and no duplicates. A prior four-vector equality-search candidate measured 0.43046 microseconds, while the selected four-accumulator parent with a one-vector search measured 0.52660 microseconds; because those programs differ in more than the search loop, this does not establish that unrolling caused the difference. This candidate preserves the selected parent's first-pass reduction and tests whether checking eight vectors per search iteration further reduces loop and mask-check overhead. It may instead waste loads when a match occurs early, so the effect may differ between random and decreasing inputs.

memory_lessons.applicability: The four-vector search result motivates testing search-loop grouping, but its first-pass implementation also differed from the selected parent, so it does not isolate the effect of unrolling.
memory_lessons.claim: A valid four-vector equality-search candidate measured 4.3046e-7 seconds, compared with 5.2559e-7 seconds for the valid single-accumulator, one-vector-search candidate. These measurements alone do not identify which source difference accounts for the observed gap.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure this eight-vector search candidate for correctness and repeated timings, paying particular attention to random and decreasing inputs.

data.notes: Only the equality-search loop changes from the selected parent: it checks eight complete vectors in index order, then handles remaining vectors and the scalar tail. The full batch boundary prevents out-of-range vector loads. No commands, build, or measurements were run; the controller must validate correctness and build compatibility on the frozen target before comparing timings.
transformations: Preserve the parent's four-accumulator signed AVX-512 first-pass minimum reduction and scalar tail.
Check equality masks for eight consecutive complete vectors per second-pass iteration, choosing the earliest vector and lowest matching lane.
Scan any remaining complete vectors and then the scalar tail, preserving bounds safety and the first-index tie rule for all valid lengths.
